description: We were a little bored so we decided to solve a world-level problem as a weekend activity.
summary: SPHEREx Sky Time Machine is a free website that turns NASA’s SPHEREx infrared survey into short videos of the sky. SPHEREx photographs the whole sky in 102 infrared colours every six months, but its data comes as hundreds of separate image files per spot, which NASA’s archive shows one at a time. Our pipeline finds every SPHEREx photo of a position, removes bad pixels and the glow of solar-system dust, lines the photos up on one grid, and stacks each six-month sky pass into a video frame. The website plays these frames like a flip-book, with a “what changed” view that makes moving or brightening objects stand out. Clicking a target shows its spectrum across all colours and how its brightness changed. Known stars from Gaia and WISE are drawn on top to check what is new. Tested on real data, it recovered all 14 sightings of two known fast-moving stars and confirmed a pulsating star’s change. A faint, slowly moving Planet X or a cold brown dwarf would look just like this. Our tool lets students, citizen scientists and researchers look for them, no code needed.
details:
What it does. SPHEREx Sky Time Machine plays NASA SPHEREx infrared photos of one spot in the sky as a short video, so anything that moves or changes brightness stands out. For any position, our Python pipeline asks NASA’s IRSA archive for every SPHEREx photo that covers it and downloads only the patch it needs. It removes bad pixels and the glow of solar-system dust, lines every photo up on one north-up grid, and averages each six-month sky pass into one video frame. The website offers a flip-book, a “what changed” view, a deep stack, single-colour views, and a spectrum and light curve for each target. Known stars from Gaia and WISE are drawn on top, moved to each photo’s date.

Benefits and impact. SPHEREx data comes as hundreds of separate files per spot, which today takes code and astronomy skills to use. Our tool lets students, teachers and citizen scientists simply look. Volunteers already found brown dwarfs by flipping through older WISE photos; we bring that method to NASA’s newest survey. A faint, slow-moving Planet X would look exactly like the movers we show.

Results (real data only). The pictures line up with Gaia stars to within 0.03″. The mover finder recovered all 14 sightings of two known fast-moving stars. WISE 0855’s brightness agrees with NASA WISE. The pulsating star R Draconis changes about 1.6×, while control stars stay steady. We claim no new objects.

Tools. Python (Astropy, astroquery, reproject, NumPy, SciPy), JavaScript with React and Vite, an optional Flask API, and GitHub Pages for hosting. We worked on our own laptops with no special hardware, and used Claude (AI) with full disclosure.

Creativity. One tool shows both motion over time and make-up across 102 colours, using the same photos.

What we considered. We considered honesty first. Every light curve gives a verdict: “steady”, “changes” or “inconclusive”. Unreliable data is flagged, not hidden, and we report our limits openly. We also wanted the tool free, with no login, shareable links and plain-language explanations.
